questions.question_text: A 20-year-old male has been brought to the mental health service by his parents as he has been complaining that he has been hearing voices. During the interview with the psychiatrist, he was noted to be repeating particular words with increasing frequency. This form of psychopathology is known as
questions.explanation: This is known as palilalia, which means that a patient repeats a word with increasing frequency. It is important to differentiate this with logoclonia, which occurs when the person repeats just the last syllable of the last word. Both of these terms are examples of preservation of speech. In perseveration, mental operations are continued beyond the point at which they are relevant.

questions.question_text: A dentist proudly mentions that patients in his dental clinic are provided with a relaxing chair, ice cream and magazines to read after that they receive stressful dental procedures. Which of the following best describes the arrangement in his clinic?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is a technique used in systematic desensitization, where the antagonistic response to anxiety (i.e. relaxation) is maintained when the feared stimulus is presented.

questions.question_text: You are posted to work in a new UK-based medical school in Singapore. A nurse is not certain how to keep the following psychotropic drugs in the ward and comes to consult you. The bioavailability of which of the following psychotropic drugs is most likely to be affected by exposure to humid atmosphere?
questions.explanation:
this question is asking which of the aforementioned psychotropic drugs
is hygroscopic. A hygroscopic drug is one which attracts moisture from the
atmosphere. Phenobarbital sodium is hygroscopic. Even in the absence of light,
phenobarbital sodium is gradually degraded on exposure to a humid atmosphere. e
other psychotropic medications are coated and they are very stable compounds
because no degradation is observed by the action of heat and light.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male has been referred by his general practitioner (GP) for a psychiatric assessment. He shared with the psychiatrist that he has been uncomfortable with his gender and is determined to have a gender re-assignment operation to become a woman. Which of the following would be the most appropriate clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Transsexualism is characterised by a desire to live as a member of the opposite sex with marked discomfort with one’s own anatomic sex and an intense desire to change the body into that of the preferred sex.

questions.question_text: A medical student asks you the specific type of epilepsy most commonly associated with olfactory hallucination. Your answer should be

options.text: Medial frontal lobe lesions and complex partial seizure
Medial parietal lobe lesions and complex partial seizure
Medial parietal lobe lesions and simple partial seizure
Medial temporal lobe lesions and complex partial seizure
Medial temporal lobe lesions and simple partial seizure

correct_answer.text: Medial temporal lobe lesions and complex partial seizure

correct_answers.text: Medial temporal lobe lesions and complex partial seizure

questions.explanation: Seizures associated with medial temporal lobe lesions, known as uncinate seizures, can give rise to olfactory hallucinations.

questions.question_text: Based on your understanding about neurosis and anxiety disorders in general, which of the following phobias has a strong underlying genetic linkage?
questions.explanation: Blood injection phobia (often involving needles and medical procedures) has been demonstrated to have a strong genetic component.

questions.question_text: You are posted to work in Kenya. There is a lot of sunlight in the daytime and the hospital does not have an air-conditioned room to keep the psychotropic medications. The bioavailability of which of the following psychotropic drugs is most likely to be affected by exposure to air and light?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine is photosensitive and hygroscopic, so exposure to air and light can reduce its bioavailability.

questions.question_text: Paramnesia refers to a distorted recall leading to falsification of memory. The feeling of 'being there before' is best described by which of the following terms?
questions.explanation: Déjà vu describes the illusion of having already experienced the current situation.

questions.question_text: A 37-year-old woman is diagnosed with depression. She feels miserable and thinks that her job requires her working long, stressful hours with brash and unfriendly colleagues. Although she is aware of the poor working environment, she does not do anything to better her situation and remains in the same job for many years. Which of the following statements about the above phenomenon is incorrect?

options.text: This phenomenon occurs when reinforcement is not contingent on behaviour.
This phenomenon is the result of a history of repeated failures.
This phenomenon is an example of classical conditioning.
There is a feeling of having no personal control over events.
This phenomenon was described by Seligman.

correct_answer.text: This phenomenon is an example of classical conditioning.

correct_answers.text: This phenomenon is an example of classical conditioning.

questions.explanation: Learned helplessness arises from repeated failure and lack of contingency between behaviour and outcome; it is not an example of classical conditioning.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man suffers from treatment-resistant schizoaffective disorder and takes clozapine. Which of the following psychotropic drugs is contraindicated as an augmentation?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine plus clozapine carries a high risk of blood dyscrasia and is contraindicated.

questions.question_text: Which of the following risk factors is associated with the highest risk of developing agranulocytosis in schizophrenic patients taking clozapine?
questions.explanation: Female gender, Ashkenazi Jewish descent and older age are key risk factors for clozapine-induced agranulocytosis.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female has been very concerned about her son Thomas. She has received feedback from his teachers at school that he has been very rigid in his duties and is not able to participate in group work as he cannot delegate tasks. He consistently seeks perfectionism in all that he does. Which of the following is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Obsessive–compulsive personality disorder is characterised by perfectionism, rigidity and an inability to delegate.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a good prognostic factor for an individual with anorexia nervosa (AN)?

options.text: Onset younger than the age of 15
Lower weight at onset and at presentation
Frequent vomiting and the presence of bulimia

correct_answer.text: Onset younger than the age of 15

correct_answers.text: Onset younger than the age of 15

questions.explanation: An early onset (before age 15) is associated with a better prognosis in anorexia nervosa.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman complains about generalized headache which has gotten worse over the past 3 weeks. Her GP thought that she suffers from tension headache. Which of the following symptoms suggest an underlying serious pathology?

options.text: Headache which bands around the head
Headache getting worse when lying down

correct_answer.text: Headache getting worse when lying down

correct_answers.text: Headache getting worse when lying down

questions.explanation: A headache that worsens on lying down suggests raised intracranial pressure and warrants further investigation.

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old boy is brought by his parents for assessment. His parents complain that he has abnormalities in reciprocal social interaction and restricted interest in buses. He was speaking fluently at the age of 2. Physical examination shows stereotyped movement and motor clumsiness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asperger’s syndrome is marked by impaired social interaction and restricted interests without early speech delay.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regards to the psychopathology that a patient is experiencing when he keeps repeating everything that the examiner has been saying?
questions.explanation: Echolalia is the automatic imitation of another’s speech.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: Second-order conditioning is the basis for single-object phobia.
Animal phobias have the best prognosis among the various phobias.
Punishment is a component of aversion therapy.
Second-order conditioning is more easily demonstrated than classical conditioning.
Forward conditioning is more used than backward conditioning.

correct_answer.text: Second-order conditioning is more easily demonstrated than classical conditioning.

correct_answers.text: Second-order conditioning is more easily demonstrated than classical conditioning.

questions.explanation: Classical (first-order) conditioning is more easily demonstrated than second-order conditioning, which requires prior learning.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man suffers from treatment-resistant schizophrenia and has started clozapine for 1 week. He refuses to have the weekly full blood count but is keen to continue clozapine. His GP is concerned that he will develop agranulocytosis and wants to find out when is the peak period for developing agranulocytosis. Your answer is
questions.explanation: The peak incidence of clozapine-induced agranulocytosis occurs in the third month of treatment.

questions.question_text: A 1-year-old child should be fearful of
questions.explanation: By about one year of age, infants typically develop a fear of loud noises.

questions.question_text: A newborn baby possesses all of the following visual characteristics except

options.text: Ability to discriminate the level of brightness
Ability to focus on an object at a distance of 0.2 m

questions.explanation: Depth perception develops by 2 months of age; newborns lack true depth perception.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man has an infarct in the anterior cerebral artery. Which of the following neurological signs is most likely to be found?
questions.explanation: Anterior cerebral artery infarction classically causes contralateral motor deficit affecting the lower limb more than the upper limb.

questions.question_text: A concerned mother brought her 5-year-old son for assessment because she worries he has developmental delay. Which of the following developmental tasks is mainly achieved at 5 years but not in earlier years?

options.text: The child is able to count age on hand.
The child is able to imitate a drawing of a circle and a cross.
The child is able to name items at home.
The child is able to run on tiptoes.

correct_answer.text: The child is able to run on tiptoes.

correct_answers.text: The child is able to run on tiptoes.

questions.explanation: Running on tiptoes typically emerges around 5 years of age; earlier gross motor milestones appear by age 3–4.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the diagnostic criteria for post-schizophrenic depression is false?

options.text: Based on DSM-IV-TR criteria, post-schizophrenic depression is not a diagnostic entity.
Based on ICD-10 criteria, the general criteria for schizophrenia must have been met within the previous 12 months prior to onset of depressive episode.
Based on ICD-10 criteria, a depressive episode instead of post-schizophrenic depression should be diagnosed if the patient no longer has any schizophrenic symptoms for a long time.
Based on ICD-10 criteria, dysthymia is severe enough to meet diagnostic criteria of post-schizophrenic depression.
The post-schizophrenic depressive episodes are associated with an increased risk of suicide.

correct_answer.text: Based on ICD-10 criteria, dysthymia is severe enough to meet diagnostic criteria of post-schizophrenic depression.

correct_answers.text: Based on ICD-10 criteria, dysthymia is severe enough to meet diagnostic criteria of post-schizophrenic depression.

questions.explanation: Dysthymia does not reach the severity threshold for post-schizophrenic depression under ICD-10; the depressive episode must meet full criteria.

questions.question_text: Which of the following types of schizophrenia is not found in the DSM-IV-TR?
questions.explanation: Hebephrenic schizophrenia (hebephrenia) is recognised in ICD-10 but not listed as a subtype in DSM-IV-TR.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a bad prognostic factor for individuals with AN?
questions.explanation: Female gender is not a poor prognostic indicator in anorexia nervosa; other listed factors predict worse outcomes.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman reports that she is the prime minister’s sister. When asked what makes her think this, she replies that it is true without further elaboration. Her affect was flat without pressure of speech. Collateral history of her family reveals that she has no relationship with the prime minister and the realization came to her ‘out of the blue’. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation: An autochthonous (primary) delusion arises suddenly and without understandable antecedent, often ‘out of the blue.’

questions.question_text: Gestalt principle is based on the following, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Three-dimensional similarity is not a recognised Gestalt grouping principle; proximity, similarity, continuity and closure are.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old schizophrenic man is prescribed clozapine at 700 mg/day. The consultant psychiatrist worries about the high risk of seizure. Which of the following anticonvulsants is the most appropriate prophylactic agent against clozapine-induced epilepsy?
questions.explanation: Valproate is the preferred prophylactic anticonvulsant for clozapine-induced seizures; carbamazepine is contraindicated.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man suffers from third-person auditory hallucination, thought interference and delusion of control for 3 months. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: He fulfils the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia based on the ICD-10.
He fulfils the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia based on DSM-IV-TR.
He fulfils the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia based on both the DSM-IV-TR and the ICD-10.
He does not fulfil diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia based on both the DSM-IV-TR and the ICD-10.

correct_answer.text: He fulfils the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia based on the ICD-10.

correct_answers.text: He fulfils the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia based on the ICD-10.

questions.explanation: ICD-10 requires only 1 month of symptoms for a schizophrenia diagnosis; DSM-IV-TR requires at least 6 months.

questions.question_text: Based on research into conformity and group behaviour, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: Within the group, member’s individual opinions were distorted based on the opinions of others in the group.
Conformity was greater in groups that had individuals who were less self-reliant.
Conformity was greater in groups that had individuals who were less intelligent.
Conformity was greater in groups that had individuals who were less self-expressive.
Conformity to the group’s decision on a line judgement experiment was greater in a group of 25 members as compared to a group of four.

correct_answer.text: Conformity to the group’s decision on a line judgement experiment was greater in a group of 25 members as compared to a group of four.

correct_answers.text: Conformity to the group’s decision on a line judgement experiment was greater in a group of 25 members as compared to a group of four.

questions.explanation: Conformity actually decreases as group size exceeds about 4–5; larger groups do not proportionally increase conformity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the theory of mind is incorrect?

options.text: In primate research, theory of mind refers to the abilities of primates to mentalize their fellows.
In humans, theory of mind refers to the ability of most normal people to comprehend the thought processes (such as attention, feelings, beliefs and knowledge) of others.
At the age of 3, normal human children do not acknowledge the false belief as they have a difficulty in differentiating belief from the world.
Cognitive changes occur at the age of 5 for children to adopt the theory of mind.
It has been suggested that a failure to acquire a theory of mind is associated with disorders such as autism.

correct_answer.text: Cognitive changes occur at the age of 5 for children to adopt the theory of mind.

correct_answers.text: Cognitive changes occur at the age of 5 for children to adopt the theory of mind.

questions.explanation: Theory of mind abilities typically emerge around age 4, not age 5.

questions.question_text: Based on the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, a patient who drinks more than what amount of caffeine is considered to be intoxicated?
questions.explanation: DSM-5 specifies that caffeine intoxication can occur with consumption in excess of 250 mg/day.

questions.question_text: The psychological therapy that deals with traps, snags and dilemmas would be
questions.explanation: Cognitive analytical therapy integrates cognitive and analytic approaches to identify and resolve ‘traps,’ ‘snags’ and ‘dilemmas.’

questions.question_text: There have been multiple aetiologies accounting for the development of personality disorders. In particular, which of these personality disorders has the strongest genetic relationship?
questions.explanation: Schizotypal personality disorder shows the highest heritability among personality disorders.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man has a tumour in the frontal lobe. Which of the following neurological signs is most likely to be found?
questions.explanation: Frontal–basal lesions commonly cause anosmia (loss of smell).

questions.question_text: Previous research has demonstrated that when there are more people around during an emergency, the participants are less likely to help. Which of the following best describes this?
questions.explanation: The bystander effect refers to decreased likelihood of help in the presence of multiple bystanders.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male has treatment-resistant schizophrenia and has been sectioned for inpatient hospitalization on multiple occasions. He has just been started on clozapine, but he has been complaining of a change in the tone of his upper limbs. Which of the following terminology best describes the psychopathology that he has been experiencing?
questions.explanation: Cenesthesia refers to an abnormal sensation of internal bodily tone or state.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old African man is referred to you for psychiatric assessment after he attempted to attack his wife. He believes that his wife has been unfaithful to him and she is having an affair with a Caucasian man. He has been trying for 1 year to prove this belief despite her repeated denial and reassurance from friends and relatives. His attempts included following her, searching her mobile phone, confronting her and checking her clothes. Which of the following aetiological factors is least likely to be associated with his condition?
questions.explanation: Delusional misidentification syndromes are a separate group of psychotic misidentification phenomena and are not typically associated with Othello (morbid jealousy) syndrome.

questions.question_text: Based on Bandura model of learning, all of the following are crucial steps in the modelling process, with the exception of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Bandura’s four key steps are attention, retention, reproduction and motivation; insight is not one of them.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered to be a theory of interpersonal attraction?
questions.explanation: Conditioning theory per se is not listed among the classic theories of interpersonal attraction; reinforcement, social exchange, equity and proxemics are.

questions.question_text: An examiner asks a person to move his arm in different directions and the person is unable to resist even if it is against her will. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Automatic obedience involves blind, automatic compliance with examiner’s commands.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old female has just given birth to a baby boy 5 days ago. She has been afraid to care for her newborn, as she has been hearing voices of the devil telling her nasty things about her child. She believes that the child has been placed under a curse by the devil. Which of the following would be the most appropriate clinical diagnosis for her?
questions.explanation: Postnatal psychosis presents in the first 2 weeks postpartum with hallucinations, delusions and rapid mood swings.

questions.question_text: A voluntary organization is attempting to recruit more volunteers to help them. They first started by asking the new volunteers to help out in a once-off charity event. Thereafter, they started to ask the volunteers to commit more of their time in helping out the organization. Which of the following techniques best describes this?
questions.explanation: Foot in the door technique involves securing a small initial commitment before asking for a larger request.

questions.question_text: When the examiner is attempting passively to move the arm of an 80-year-old man with dementia, the examiner feels that the patient is applying the same amount of force in resisting the passive movement. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Gegenhalten is uneven, variable resistance to passive movement, seen in frontal lobe disease and dementia.

questions.question_text: A medical student was asked to examine a patient and determine what pathology he has. On neurological examination, it was noted that the patient is unable to cooperate and looks downwards and laterally. He complains of double vision when attempting to do so. This is most likely due to a lesion involving
questions.explanation: The fourth cranial nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle, which depresses and intorts the eye in adduction; its palsy causes diplopia on downward gaze.

questions.question_text: Aggression has been described as a behaviour intended to harm others. There are various explanations for aggressive behaviours. Which of the following is incorrect?

options.text: Aggression is perceived to be a learnt response, from previous observation, imitation and operant conditioning.
Victim suffering and material gains will reinforce subsequent aggressive behaviour.
The consequences of aggression usually play a role in determining future aggression.
Behaviours such as maintaining a distance, evoking a social response incompatible with aggression and familiarity will help to inhibit aggression.
Emotional arousal might or might not increase aggression.

correct_answer.text: Emotional arousal might or might not increase aggression.

correct_answers.text: Emotional arousal might or might not increase aggression.

questions.explanation: Emotional arousal typically increases the likelihood and intensity of aggressive behaviour.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man was brought to the Accident and Emergency Department. He suddenly fell down after hearing a loud sound at a party. There was no loss of consciousness. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation: Cataplexy is sudden muscle weakness or collapse triggered by strong emotion, without loss of consciousness.

questions.question_text: Which of the following movement disorders is not typically associated with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Mannerisms are purposeless, odd gestures seen in catatonia but not characteristically in schizophrenia alone.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man suffers from schizophrenia and he has been taking chlorpromazine for the past 20 years. You are the consultant psychiatrist and reviewing his drug list because you are concerned of drug interaction. Which of the following drug interactions is the most significant?

options.text: Amitriptyline decreases the serum concentration of chlorpromazine.
Chlorpromazine decreases the serum concentration of amitriptyline.
Chlorpromazine increases the serum concentration of amitriptyline.
Chlorpromazine decreases the serum concentration of valproate.
Chlorpromazine increases the serum concentration of valproate.

correct_answer.text: Chlorpromazine increases the serum concentration of valproate.

correct_answers.text: Chlorpromazine increases the serum concentration of valproate.

questions.explanation: Chlorpromazine inhibits valproate metabolism, thereby increasing valproate serum levels.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female has been diagnosed with a previous psychiatric condition. Her symptoms have remitted over the past 2 years, but recently due to increased stress at work, she has been resorting to measures to cope with stress. One of the methods she has been using is to restrict her diet, in order to reduce her body mass index from the current of 20 to 15. What form of psychological therapy would be the most useful and beneficial for her?
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural therapy is first-line for eating disorders, targeting distorted thoughts about weight, body image and eating behaviours.

questions.question_text: Which of the following aphasia resembles speech disturbances that schizophrenic patients have?
questions.explanation: In jargon aphasia the patient utters incoherent, meaningless neologistic speech, resembling thought disorder in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Schemas help to influence the way people organize knowledge about the social world and also help them to interpret new situations. All of the following about schemas are incorrect with the exception of

options.text: Schemas tend to slow down the rate of mental processing.
Schemas are not likely to be helpful when dealing with an ambiguous situation.
Schemas usually require more effortful thinking.
Schemas tend to persist even after evidence for the schema has been discredited.
Schemas play a part in maintaining prejudice.

correct_answer.text: Schemas tend to persist even after evidence for the schema has been discredited.

correct_answers.text: Schemas tend to persist even after evidence for the schema has been discredited.

questions.explanation: Schemas often persist despite disconfirming evidence because they are entrenched and activated automatically under limited cognitive resources.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted to the psychiatric ward. The nurse informs you that he always protrudes his lips, which resemble a snout. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation: Schnauzkrampf is a snout-like protrusion of the lips seen in catatonic schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male, Thomas, was at his father’s funeral, helping to carry his father’s coffin when he developed an acute onset of bilateral blindness. The medical team doctors have seen him, and they have found nothing medically wrong. He has also been seen by the on-call psychiatrist, to which he reports feeling indifferent to the blindness. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Conversion disorder presents with neurological symptoms (e.g., blindness) incompatible with organic pathology, often with 'la belle indifference.'

questions.question_text: All of the following are known clinical features of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Hypothermia is not a feature of Wernicke’s encephalopathy; the classic triad includes ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes fundamental attribution error?

options.text: Attributing others’ mistakes to the context in which the mistakes occur
Attributing one’s own mistakes to one’s character and personality
Refusing to accept one’s own errors
Denying the fundamental flaws behind one’s own negative behaviour
Attributing others’ mistakes to their personal dispositions

correct_answer.text: Attributing others’ mistakes to their personal dispositions

correct_answers.text: Attributing others’ mistakes to their personal dispositions

questions.explanation: Fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overestimate dispositional factors and underestimate situational factors when explaining others’ behaviours.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man suffers from prostate cancer and was admitted to the hospital for chemotherapy. He developed nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy. Whenever he sees the hospital building, he feels nauseated. He has completed chemotherapy and is not required to return to the hospital. The nausea feeling disappears. The disappearance of nausea feeling is known as
questions.explanation: Extinction is the gradual disappearance of a conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is presented without the unconditioned stimulus.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man suffers from prostate cancer and he was admitted to the hospital for chemotherapy. He developed nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy. Two months later, he feels nausea when he sees the hospital building. The nausea feeling associated with the hospital building is known as
questions.explanation: The nausea in response to the hospital building (previously paired with chemotherapy) is a conditioned response.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man sets a daily alarm on his mobile phone to remind him to take his medication, Drug A. He constantly experiences side effects whenever he takes Drug A, which includes nausea. After some time, when he hears a similar alarm from his alarm clock, he also experiences nausea. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Stimulus generalization occurs when a stimulus similar to the original conditioned stimulus elicits the conditioned response.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman meets the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia and exhibits first-rank symptoms. First-rank symptoms include the following except
questions.explanation: Delusion of persecution is a second-rank symptom; first-rank symptoms are more pathognomonic (e.g., passivity phenomena, insertion, withdrawal, broadcast, delusional perception).

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old woman with a history of depression presents with bilateral ptosis. Which of the following conditions is least likely?
questions.explanation: Levator palpebrae muscle paralysis typically causes unilateral ptosis; bilateral ptosis suggests a systemic neuromuscular disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not true about fundamental attribution error?

options.text: Seen in adults in western societies
Bias towards attributing a behaviour to situational causes

correct_answer.text: Bias towards attributing a behaviour to situational causes

correct_answers.text: Bias towards attributing a behaviour to situational causes

questions.explanation: Fundamental attribution error is a bias toward attributing others’ behaviour to personal dispositions, not situational causes.

questions.question_text: A public health official wants to consult you on the use of APOE alleles as a screening test to identify individuals with a high chance to develop Alzheimer’s disease and offer early intervention. Which of the following is true about APOE screening test?

options.text: Low positive predictive value; low negative predictive value; low sensitivity and low specificity
Low positive predictive value; high negative predictive value; low sensitivity and low specificity
Low positive predictive value; high negative predictive value; high sensitivity and low specificity
Low positive predictive value; high negative predictive value; high sensitivity and high specificity
High positive predictive value; high negative predictive value; high sensitivity and high specificity

correct_answer.text: Low positive predictive value; low negative predictive value; low sensitivity and low specificity

correct_answers.text: Low positive predictive value; low negative predictive value; low sensitivity and low specificity

questions.explanation: APOE screening has low PPV, low NPV, low sensitivity and low specificity, making it unsuitable for population screening.

questions.question_text: A medical student attached to the Consultation–Liaison team asked the consultant psychiatrist which of the following would be the earliest and most reliable sign to differentiate between dementia and delirium. The correct answer would be

options.text: Presence of focal neurological signs on clinical examination

questions.explanation: Altered consciousness (fluctuating level of alertness) is the hallmark of delirium, distinguishing it from dementia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best way to prevent dementia?

options.text: Offer genetic testing to older adults
Treat systolic hypertension (>160 mm Hg) in older people (age >60 years)

correct_answer.text: Treat systolic hypertension (>160 mm Hg) in older people (age >60 years)

correct_answers.text: Treat systolic hypertension (>160 mm Hg) in older people (age >60 years)

questions.explanation: Treating systolic hypertension in older adults has the best evidence for dementia prevention; other strategies lack definitive benefit.

questions.question_text: The consultant psychiatrist shows his medical students a video on interviewing a schizophrenic patient, and mentions to them that the patient in the video has the full set of all the first-rank symptoms. Which of the following should the consultant psychiatrist clarify with the students and tell them that it is not considered as a first-rank symptom?
questions.explanation: Thought block (sudden interruption of thought) is not one of Schneider’s classic first-rank symptoms.

questions.question_text: Peri-trauma factors that predispose an individual to develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) include all of the following except

options.text: Perceived lack of social support during the trauma

correct_answer.text: Perceived lack of social support during the trauma

correct_answers.text: Perceived lack of social support during the trauma

questions.explanation: Perceived lack of social support is a post-trauma risk factor, not peri-trauma.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines social psychology?

options.text: The scientific study of the way in which people’s thoughts, feelings and behaviours are influenced by the real, imagined or implied presence of other people
The scientific study of how people’s behaviours, thoughts and feelings are influenced by the social environment
The scientific study of how people’s behaviours, thoughts and feelings are influenced by society
The scientific study of behaviour and mental processes
The scientific study of how behaviours are influenced by mental processes

correct_answer.text: The scientific study of the way in which people’s thoughts, feelings and behaviours are influenced by the real, imagined or implied presence of other people

correct_answers.text: The scientific study of the way in which people’s thoughts, feelings and behaviours are influenced by the real, imagined or implied presence of other people

questions.explanation: Social psychology focuses on how individuals are influenced by the real, imagined or implied presence of others.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman is referred by her dermatologist to see you. She complains of pruritus as a result of an infestation with parasites. She shows you her debris contained in plastic wrap and claims that it contains the parasites. The patient is most likely suffering from
questions.explanation: Ekbom syndrome (delusional parasitosis) involves the false belief of infestation and the 'matchbox sign' (bringing debris).

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man sets a daily alarm on his mobile phone to remind him to take his medication, Drug A. He constantly experiences side effects whenever he takes Drug A, which includes nausea. After some time, when he hears a similar alarm from his alarm clock, he also experiences nausea. However, this phenomenon disappears after a few days. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation:
Stimulus discrimination refers to the tendency to stop responding to the
stimulus similar to the conditioned stimulus, as the similar stimulus is not paired with
the unconditioned stimulus. the man learns to differentiate or discriminate between
the two alarm sounds and learns to respond differently to each alarm.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man sets a daily alarm on his mobile phone to remind him to take his medication, Drug A. He constantly experiences side effects whenever he takes Drug A, which includes nausea. After changing his medication to Drug B, he stops experiencing nausea. However, after a few days, he again starts to feel nauseated when he hears his mobile phone alarm. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a conditioned response after a pause following extinction.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man has a lesion in the left occipital lobe. Which of the following signs is most likely to be found?
questions.explanation: Alexia without agraphia ('dyslexia without agraphia') results from occipital–splenial disconnection, allowing writing but not reading.

questions.question_text: Which of the following trials or tests led to public outrage and request from Queen Victoria to clarify the legal standard in the 1840s?
questions.explanation: The M’Naghten trial (1843) led to the establishment of the M’Naghten rules for legal insanity.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male presented to the mental health services as he has been feeling low for the past 2 months. The low mood is associated with diminished interests, feelings that life is not worth going on and biological symptoms such as poor sleep and appetite. Which of the following descriptors best describes the severity of his underlying depression?
questions.explanation:
Based on the ICD-10 diagnostic classi cation system, he is likely to be
suffering from moderate degree of depression. Duration of 2 weeks of symptoms is
required for the diagnosis. this applies to the rst episode only. Severity is classi ed
into mild depressive disorder, moderate depressive disorder, severe depressive episode
without psychotic symptoms and severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms.

questions.question_text: A 38-year-old father is diagnosed with schizophrenia. His wife does not have any psychiatric illness. He wants to know the risk of his son developing the disorder. Your answer is
questions.explanation: The lifetime risk for a child with one schizophrenic parent is about 10%.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male is extremely upset that his son has been sectioned for admission for psychosis. He knows that it might be due to the drugs – cannabis which his son has been using. Cannabis is known to increase the incidences of psychosis by approximately how much percent?
questions.explanation: Heavy cannabis use confers about a fourfold increased risk of psychosis.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old female Sally is concerned whether her brother who has Down’s syndrome would develop psychosis. Based on the current research evidence, the risk of her brother developing schizophrenia has been estimated to be

options.text: The same as the normal population.
There has been found to be an association, but there is no strong evidence to support the estimated increment in risk.

correct_answer.text: There has been found to be an association, but there is no strong evidence to support the estimated increment in risk.

correct_answers.text: There has been found to be an association, but there is no strong evidence to support the estimated increment in risk.

questions.explanation: Although Down’s syndrome is linked to early-onset Alzheimer’s, schizophrenia risk is not clearly elevated.

questions.question_text: A 6-year-old girl has a fear of injections but requires frequent injections. She has to consult with a doctor before getting her injection. She recognizes her doctor by his white coat. After her consultation with the doctor, she has to wait for her turn in the waiting area before proceeding to another room for her injection. Soon, whenever she sees a doctor’s white coat, she reports feeling scared and anxious. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Trace conditioning occurs when the conditioned stimulus precedes the unconditioned stimulus with a delay; here the white coat precedes the injection.

questions.question_text: The term ‘schizoaffective psychosis’ was introduced by Kasanin in which of the following decades?
questions.explanation: Kasanin coined the term schizoaffective psychosis in 1933.

questions.question_text: Based on the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) guidelines in the UK, how long must a bipolar patient be stable and well before being allowed to drive again?
questions.explanation: Patients with bipolar disorder requiring admission should be off the road for 6 months after recovery.

questions.question_text: The relative risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease in a 55-year-old patient with Down’s syndrome has been estimated to be
questions.explanation: Individuals with Down’s syndrome age 50–59 have a 35%–40% risk of Alzheimer’s pathology.

questions.question_text: Deinstitutionalization peaked in the 1970s. Which of the following statements is not associated with deinstitutionalization?

options.text: People with mental illnesses are not at a higher risk of offending compared to the general population.
Increase in awareness of civil rights of people with mental illnesses.
Increase in costs of institutionalization care.
Reduction in availability of hospital beds.

correct_answer.text: People with mental illnesses are not at a higher risk of offending compared to the general population.

correct_answers.text: People with mental illnesses are not at a higher risk of offending compared to the general population.

questions.explanation: Post-deinstitutionalization, mentally ill individuals in the community have been found at higher risk of offending and victimization.

questions.question_text: An 8-year-old girl has a phobia of spiders. When she is presented with a spider, it elicits high levels of fear and anxiety. The experimenter plays a ringing sound at the same time and for the duration of the presentation of the spider. The experimenter is hoping to elicit similar feelings of fear and anxiety when the girl hears the ringing sound without the presentation of the spider. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: In simultaneous conditioning the conditioned stimulus and unconditioned stimulus are presented together.

questions.question_text: Based on your understanding about the history of schizophrenia, the concept that schizophrenia developed from a split mind was proposed by
questions.explanation: Bleuler introduced the term schizophrenia (from 'schizo' = split, 'phrenia' = mind) in 1911.

questions.question_text: Schizoaffective disorder was a disorder introduced by the following individual:
questions.explanation: Kasanin first described schizoaffective psychosis, noting both affective and schizophrenic features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false with regards to the consequentialist approach?

options.text: An action is moral if it makes the greatest number of people happy.
Different treatment options can be measured by foreseeable consequences such as quality-adjusted life years (QALYs).
In managed mental health care, the consequentialist approach may lead to discrimination of individual patients and moral dilemmas owing to factual uncertainties.
It is based on an obligation of fidelity (including a pledge for confidentiality), deontological theory and virtue ethics.
Under the consequentialist approach, confidentiality is an absolute condition in psychiatric practice.

correct_answer.text: Under the consequentialist approach, confidentiality is an absolute condition in psychiatric practice.

correct_answers.text: Under the consequentialist approach, confidentiality is an absolute condition in psychiatric practice.

questions.explanation: Consequentialism allows breaching confidentiality if doing so yields the best overall outcomes; it is not absolute.

questions.question_text: You are assigned to provide tutorial to four medical students. Each student needs to write a case report for a psychiatric patient. One student is confused about the meaning of mental state examination (MSE). Which of the following statements is true?

options.text: The Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) is a shorter version of the Mental State Examination.
MSE provides important information in establishing a psychiatric diagnosis.
MSE should be conducted after history taking.
The student does not need to report any physical finding because MSE has replaced physical examination in psychiatry.
When there is a discrepancy between information from the history and findings at the MSE, the student should establish the diagnosis based on the information from the history.

correct_answer.text: MSE provides important information in establishing a psychiatric diagnosis.

correct_answers.text: MSE provides important information in establishing a psychiatric diagnosis.

questions.explanation: The MSE yields objective observations (appearance, behavior, speech, mood, thought content/process, cognition) crucial for diagnosis.

questions.question_text: You are interviewing a woman who was diagnosed with schizophrenia. You think that she may suffer from other psychiatric disorders as her first-rank symptoms are inconsistent. Which of the following features is not typically associated with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
the presence of emotional labiality suggests the diagnosis of bipolar
disorder

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia says, 'The community psychiatric nurse syringe risperidone me fortnightly.' This psychopathology is known as
questions.explanation: Neologism is the creation of a new word or phrase, here condensing 'syringe' and 'risperidone.'

questions.question_text: Based on the ICD-10 diagnostic and classification criteria, the diagnosis of delusional disorder could be made only if the symptoms have lasted for at least the past
questions.explanation: ICD-10 requires at least 3 months of persistent delusions for delusional disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the genetics of AN is correct?

options.text: Less than 5% of first-degree relatives are usually affected.
Linkage genes on chromosome 3 have been found.
The ratio for monozygotic (MZ) to dizygotic (DZ) concordance is around 56:5.
Research has found the concordance rates for monozygotic twins to be the same as that for dizygotic twins.

correct_answer.text: The ratio for monozygotic (MZ) to dizygotic (DZ) concordance is around 56:5.

correct_answers.text: The ratio for monozygotic (MZ) to dizygotic (DZ) concordance is around 56:5.

questions.explanation: Twin studies show a ~56% concordance in MZ twins vs ~5% in DZ twins, indicating strong heritability.

questions.question_text: The mother of a 21-year-old male, who has just been diagnosed with OCD, wonders which of the following compulsions is the most common amongst adults. Which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: Checking rituals (e.g., doors, appliances) are the most prevalent compulsions in adult OCD.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female has been dependent on medications to help her with her anxiety condition. Recently, her psychiatrist removed one of the chronic medications that she used to be taking. This has resulted in the following withdrawal symptoms: autonomic hyperactivity, malaise and weakness, tinnitus and grand mal convulsions. Which of the following is the most likely clinical diagnosis for her?
questions.explanation: Abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause autonomic instability, malaise, tinnitus and seizures.

questions.question_text: The Folstein’s MMSE includes all of the following items except

options.text: Drawing the face of a clock, indicating 10 past 11
Orientation to time, place and person

correct_answer.text: Drawing the face of a clock, indicating 10 past 11

correct_answers.text: Drawing the face of a clock, indicating 10 past 11

questions.explanation: Clock drawing is not part of the Mini–Mental State Examination; it is used in other cognitive tests.

questions.question_text: A Greenland Inuit woman suddenly strips off her clothes and rolls in the snow followed by echolalia and echopraxia. She has no recollection of the episode afterwards. This woman suffers from which of the following culture-bound syndromes?
questions.explanation: Pibloktoq (Arctic hysteria) involves sudden dissociative episodes with hyperactivity, echolalia, echopraxia and post-episode amnesia.

questions.question_text: What was the implication of Tarasoff I (1974)?
questions.explanation: Tarasoff I established a therapist’s duty to warn identifiable victims of a patient’s threat.

questions.question_text: What was the implication of Tarasoff II (1976)?
questions.explanation: Tarasoff II expanded this to a duty to protect potential victims by reasonable means, not just warn them.

questions.question_text: An Inuit living in the Arctic Circle complains of sudden paralysis when he slept. He recalls that he was very agitated during the paralysis. The day before the attack, he could hear transient and unusual sound in his neighbourhood. He attributes the unusual experience to spirit possession. This man suffers from which of the following culture-bound syndromes?
questions.explanation: Uqamairineq in Inuit culture involves sleep paralysis with agitation and hallucinations attributed to spirits.

questions.question_text: A 6-year-old boy has phobia of snakes. When he is presented with a snake, it elicits high levels of fear and anxiety. The experimenter plays a ringing sound after the presentation of the snake. The experimenter is hoping to elicit similar feelings of fear and anxiety when the boy hears the ringing sound without the presentation of the snake. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Backward conditioning presents the conditioned stimulus after the unconditioned stimulus and is generally less effective than forward conditioning.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of pseudobulbar palsy?

options.text: Upper motor neuron lesions as a result of bilateral lesions above the mid-pons

questions.explanation: In pseudobulbar palsy, the jaw jerk is brisk (hyperactive), not normal.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is correct?

options.text: A score of 21 or above is considered normal.
MoCA has lower sensitivity compared to the MMSE in identifying mild cognitive impairment.
MoCA is available in English and French only.
The short-term memory recall task involves two learning trials of ten nouns and delayed recall after approximately 20 minutes.
Visuospatial abilities are assessed using a clock-drawing task and a three-dimensional cube copy.

correct_answer.text: Visuospatial abilities are assessed using a clock-drawing task and a three-dimensional cube copy.

correct_answers.text: Visuospatial abilities are assessed using a clock-drawing task and a three-dimensional cube copy.

questions.explanation: Visuospatial abilities are assessed using a clock-drawing task and a three-dimensional cube copy.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old African university student has been preparing for a pharmacology examination and presents with a burning headache, blurred vision, difficulty in understanding the meaning of the textbook and an inability to remember the drugs he studied. This man suffers from which of the following culture-bound syndromes?
questions.explanation: Brain fag refers to brain fatigue from too much thinking demanded of students. Brain fag is a culture-bound syndrome in West Africa.

questions.question_text: The most common defence mechanism seen in paranoid personality disorder is
questions.explanation: A person with paranoid personality disorder often projects the tendency to harm others and believes that others are trying to harm him or her.

questions.question_text: The case Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California is related to which of the following ethical principles:
questions.explanation: In Tarasoff I (1974) and II (1976) the court held that mental health professionals have a duty to warn/protect potential victims, which necessarily breaches patient confidentiality.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old Chinese national serviceman in Singapore complains that his penis is getting shorter and that it will continue to retract into his abdomen. He measures his penis every day and he cannot concentrate on his work. This man suffers from which of the following culture-bound syndromes?
questions.explanation: Koro refers to an acute panic or anxiety reaction involving fear of genital retraction.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old female has had a previous episode of depression 2 years ago. Currently, she presents with hypomania. Which clinical diagnosis is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Bipolar disorder type II requires at least one major depressive episode and at least one hypomanic episode; there is no full mania.

questions.question_text: A core trainee wants to know more about the Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination—Revised (ACE-R). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The ACE-R does not incorporate MMSE.
The ACE-R is available in Cantonese for Hong Kong patients.
The cut-off score gives rise to high sensitivity and 100% specificity for diagnosing dementia.
The cut-off score gives rise to high specificity and 100% sensitivity for diagnosing dementia.
It is a cognitive test commonly used for screening delirium.

correct_answer.text: The cut-off score gives rise to high sensitivity and 100% specificity for diagnosing dementia.

correct_answers.text: The cut-off score gives rise to high sensitivity and 100% specificity for diagnosing dementia.

questions.explanation: Using a cut-off of 82 on the ACE-R yields a sensitivity of 84% and 100% specificity for dementia.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman admitted under your care appears arrogant, refuses to follow ward rules and insists on drinking alcohol in the ward. She believes she is “special” and exploits others. Which defence mechanism is least commonly used by people with her disorder?
questions.explanation: This presentation is typical of narcissistic personality disorder; suppression is least characteristic.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man treated with chemotherapy developed nausea and vomiting after each session. Whenever he sees the hospital building he feels nauseated, and later when he sees a white coat he also feels nausea. The nausea associated with the white coat is called
questions.explanation: This is second-order conditioning: the white coat is a new CS learned via the original conditioned stimulus (the hospital).

questions.question_text: Based on the ACE-R scale, which cut-off score is the most specific for dementia?
questions.explanation: A cut-off of 82 gives 100% specificity for diagnosing dementia (with 84% sensitivity).

questions.question_text: A 43-year-old man is angry at being caught speeding. He goes home and yells at his wife and children. Which defence mechanism best describes this?
questions.explanation: Displacement is redirecting feelings from the original (threatening) target to a less threatening one.

questions.question_text: Patients with schizophrenia are more likely to relapse if discharged to families with high expressed emotion for more than
questions.explanation: Relapse risk is highest when families display high criticism/over-involvement for more than 33 hours/week.

questions.question_text: The anatomical correlate of a form of memory located in the visual or auditory association cortex is best described as
questions.explanation: Short-term memory for non-verbal and verbal stimuli maps to sensory/association cortices.

questions.question_text: A businessman killed in an accident; his angry son channels revenge into taking over his father’s business. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Sublimation transforms unacceptable impulses into a socially constructive activity.

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old girl is scared of monkeys. At the zoo she behaves aggressively, as if to attack the monkey. This is
questions.explanation: Reaction formation: the behaviour is the opposite of the underlying fear.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman with 6-month history of progressive dysphagia is referred for depression. She has no mood response to dysphagia and her husband confirms it. Most likely diagnosis is

options.text: Moderate depressive episode with somatic complaints

questions.explanation: Progressive worsening dysphagia suggests an organic cause; motor neuron disease is most likely.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old female says she always finds it tough to make decisions. Which personality disorder is likely?
questions.explanation: Dependent personality disorder is characterized by difficulty making everyday decisions without excessive advice.

questions.question_text: Features of catatonia include all of the following except
questions.explanation:
the clinical features of catatonia include all of the following:
ambitendency, automatic obedience, mitegehen, mitmachen, mannerism, negativism,
echolalia, echopraxia, logorrhea and stereotypy. e common etiological causes for
catatonia include schizophrenia, depression of manic (more common than
schizophrenia), organic disorders, epilepsy, medications, recreational drugs and
psychogenic catatonia.

questions.question_text: This test could be used for the assessment of dementia as well as in the assessment of childhood development and learning disability.
questions.explanation:
this is a scale that consists of 117 items that assess different aspects of
social maturity and social ability. It can be used for the assessment of dementia,
childhood development and learning disability

questions.question_text: This is a nurse-rated assessment scale.
questions.explanation:
Both the Clifton Assessment Schedule and the Stockton Geriatric Rating
Scale are scales that are used by nurses for assessment

questions.question_text: This is a questionnaire that is usually administered to a relative or friend of the patient.
questions.explanation:
this is a questionnaire that is usually administered to a relative or friend
who is asked to answer the questions on the basis of performance over the previous 6
months. the first set of questions deals with activities of daily living, the second set
deals with further activities of daily living and the third set deals with changes in
personality, interest and drive

questions.question_text: This is a semi-structured interview that assesses the subject’s mental state.
questions.explanation:
Geriatric Mental State Schedule is a semi-structured interview which
assesses the subject’s mental state.

questions.question_text: This is a questionnaire that consists of 13 computerized tasks.
questions.explanation:
this is an automated computerized task that offers sensitive and specic
cognitive assessment, using a touch screen. It consists of 13 computerized tasks

questions.question_text: This is a brief test that could be used to rapidly detect possible dementia, to follow up on the course of cognitive changes over time and to differentiate between delirium and dementia.
questions.explanation:
the answer is Mini Mental State Examination. It in itself has a clear
advantage over a combination of cognitive testing and informant questionnaire.

questions.question_text: Some frontal-lobe damaged patients may occasionally give grossly incorrect answers to known phenomena.
questions.explanation:
In the absence of a reduction of intelligence quotient (IQ), some frontal
lobe damaged patients may give outrageous incorrect cognitive estimates of commonly
known phenomena. For example, when asked to estimate the length of an adult
elephant, they might reply 100 yards.

questions.question_text: This is a strategy application test that helps to uncover evidence of organization difficulty that might have occurred as a result of frontal lobe damage.
questions.explanation:
In this test, the subject is asked to carry out six different tasks (in two
groups of three) during a quarter of an hour. In order to maximize their score, the
subject needs adequately to plan and schedule these tasks while also monitoring the
time that has elapsed

questions.question_text: The following abilities are tested in this test: sequencing, cognitive flexibility, visual scanning, spatial analysis, motor control, alertness and concentration.
questions.explanation:
the aforementioned test evaluates all of the above-mentioned abilities.
Difficulties with cognitive exibility or complex conceptual thinking may manifest as
much longer times being required for Trail B than would be expected from the Trail A
time score

questions.question_text: This is a test that helps to pick up perseverative errors.
questions.explanation:
this helps to pick up perseverative errors (such as continuing too long to
sort the cards by number, well after the indexing rule has changed to colour) and
non-perseverative errors. Poor performance on this task is particularly associated with
dysfunction of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.

questions.question_text: Left frontal lobe lesions are usually associated with poor performance on this particular test that tests for planning ability.
This is a test that involves asking the subject to articulate as many words as possible over a fixed duration of time.
questions.explanation:
A typical verbal uency test involves asking the subject to articulate as
many words as possible, during a 2-minute interval, starting with the letters F, A, S
and in turn. Proper nouns and derivatives such as plurals and different verb endings
are not allowed to count together with the root words. Verbal fluency is impaired in
left (dominant) frontal lobe lesions.

questions.question_text: This is a test that tests the interference that may occur between reading words and naming colours.
questions.explanation:
the aforementioned is true with regards to the description of this test.
Inference may occur between reading words and naming colours. Left dominant
frontal lobe lesions are associated with poor performance on the Stroop test

questions.question_text: She copes with her memory impairment by making jokes.
questions.explanation: This is an example of humour.

questions.question_text: She laughs and jokes with the trainee. Then she suddenly bursts into tears and asks for forgiveness.
questions.explanation: This example demonstrates labile affect.

questions.question_text: When a male trainee interviews her, she touches his inner thigh and wants to take off her blouse.
questions.explanation: This illustrates disinhibition. If such a scenario occurs in the CASC exam, a chaperone should be called.

questions.question_text: A patient is busy sending an SMS while the psychiatrist is talking. When asked to recall, he cannot.
questions.explanation: The patient has storage failure and cannot recall.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man hears a gunshot and suddenly remembers a long-forgotten robbery.
questions.explanation: The gunshot serves as a cue, enabling retrieval of the memory.

questions.question_text: A Canadian woman in the UK always gets into the driver’s side of her brother’s car despite reminders.
questions.explanation: Old learning (driving in Canada) proactively interferes with the new learning.

questions.question_text: This classification system was developed based on the mental disorders section of ICD-6.
questions.explanation: DSM-I (1952) was essentially based on the mental disorders section of ICD-6.

questions.question_text: This was an innovative psychiatric classification system that introduced operational criteria and multi-axial format.
questions.explanation: DSM-III (1980) introduced explicit operational criteria and a multi-axial system.

questions.question_text: Revisions were done and this was published in 1987:
questions.explanation: The DSM-III was revised as DSM-III-R in 1987.

questions.question_text: Escape conditioning is an example of this:
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement occurs when removal of an aversive stimulus increases a behaviour (escape conditioning).

questions.question_text: This refers to a situation in which an aversive stimulus is presented whenever a given behaviour occurs:
questions.explanation: Punishment is the presentation of an aversive stimulus contingent on a behaviour, reducing its future frequency.

questions.question_text: This refers to reinforcement that occurs through reduction of needs driving from basic drives:
questions.explanation: Primary reinforcement involves direct reduction of biological drives (e.g., food, water).

questions.question_text: This refers to reinforcement derived from association with primary reinforcers:
questions.explanation: Secondary reinforcers gain value through pairing with primary reinforcers (e.g., money).

questions.question_text: In this schedule of reinforcement, reinforcer is delivered only after a fixed interval of time:
questions.explanation: Fixed-interval schedules deliver reinforcement after set time periods; they produce a scallop of responses.

questions.question_text: In this schedule of reinforcement, reinforcer is delivered after variable intervals:
questions.explanation: Variable-interval schedules reinforce after unpredictable time periods, yielding a steady rate of response.

questions.question_text: This schedule of reinforcement is generally considered best for maintaining a high response rate:
questions.explanation: Fixed-ratio schedules (reinforcement after a set number of responses) produce high rates of responding.

questions.question_text: This form of attachment would predispose individuals towards childhood emotional disorders and disorders such as agoraphobia:
questions.explanation: Insecure attachment (clinginess and ambivalence) is linked to later emotional disorders.

questions.question_text: This form of attachment would predispose individuals towards poor social functioning in later life, which might include aggression:
questions.explanation: Avoidant attachment (emotional distance from the caregiver) is associated with later social difficulties and aggression.

questions.question_text: As a result of this, an infant may hold a comfort object or a transitional object:
questions.explanation:
Separation anxiety refers to the fear an infant shows of being separated
from his or her caregiver. Holding a comfort object or a transitional object would help
to deal with these feelings. the rate of disappearance of separation anxiety varies with
the child’s experiences of previous separations, handling by mother, perception of
whether the mother will die or depart and temperament.

questions.question_text: Developmental language delay, shallow relationships and lack of empathy might arise due to this
questions.explanation: Following a failure to form adequate attachments, for example due to prolonged maternal separation or rejecting parents, can lead to the development of language delay, indiscriminate affection seeking, shallow relationships, lack of empathy, aggression and social disinhibition

questions.question_text: A patient breaks down the word’s spelling and has much difficulty in writing irregular words. This is an example of
questions.explanation: This is caused by lesion in the left temporo-parietal region. The person breaks down the word’s spelling and has difficulty in writing irregular words.

questions.question_text: A patient is unable to spell non-existent words. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Deep dysgraphia is caused by extensive left hemisphere lesion and a breakdown of the sound-based route for spelling.

questions.question_text: A patient tends to misspell the initial part of words. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Neglect dysgraphia is caused by right hemispheric lesions and leads to misspelling of the initial part of words.

questions.question_text: Three months after suffering a stroke, a patient develops a new technique to help himself recognize words. He reads letter by letter and spells the word out loud. Then he recognizes the word after hearing himself spell it out. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Alexia without agraphia results from left posterior cerebral artery occlusion, producing right hemianopia and disconnection of visual input from language areas; the patient learns letter-by-letter compensatory reading.

questions.question_text: The staff of a hostel for learning disability patients wants to train her clients to clean up the tables after meals. She develops a successive reinforcing schedule to reward her clients. The clients will be rewarded successively over time for putting their utensils away from the dining table back to the pantry. Then they need to clean the utensils and put them back to the cupboard.
questions.explanation: Shaping involves reinforcing successive approximations of a desired behaviour over time.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old son is scared of dogs. His mother tries to reduce his fear by bringing him to see the dogs in the park. The fear-provoking situation is coupled and opposed by putting him on her lap and allowing him to drink his favourite juice.
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is introducing a relaxation response (juice and lap comfort) incompatible with fear.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman develops fear of the London tube and sees a psychologist. The psychologist has drafted a behavioural programme where the patient is advised to start with travelling between two tube stations with her husband and gradually increase to more stations without her husband, ending with the full route alone.
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization uses a graded hierarchy of exposures paired with relaxation.

questions.question_text: That same woman is instructed to start with the most fearful situation by taking a train from the Heathrow terminal station to the Cockfosters Station along the Piccadilly line on her own.
questions.explanation: Flooding involves immediate exposure to the highest anxiety-evoking stimulus.

questions.question_text: An 11-year-old girl is allowed to play piano for 30 minutes only after spending 1 hour on her homework.
questions.explanation: Premack’s principle uses a high-probability activity (piano) to reinforce a low-probability behaviour (homework).

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old girl is rewarded with a sticker every time she completes her homework; after 20 stickers she can exchange them for a present.
questions.explanation: A token economy awards tokens (stickers) as secondary reinforcers that can be exchanged for privileges.

questions.question_text: In prison, psychologists develop an in vivo exposure programme for prisoners to view images of arrest and social sanctions; repeated exposures reduce their urge to commit crimes.
questions.explanation:
this type of aversive conditioning is known as convert sensitization as
the prisoners imagine the adverse outcomes.

questions.question_text: A 6-year-old boy placed in a maze finds a toy box; after a few trials he learns the route and time to find the toy decreases.
questions.explanation: Latent learning is acquisition of knowledge (maze map) without explicit reinforcement.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child is toilet-trained by breaking the complex behaviour into steps: first reporting the urge, then using the toilet unaided for a sticker.
questions.explanation: Chaining teaches components of a complex behaviour in sequence until the full behaviour is learned.

questions.question_text: A hostel resident with learning disability assaults others; staff remove his TV privileges and give him a 2-hour time-out.
questions.explanation: Penalty involves removal of a positive stimulus (TV) contingent on undesirable behaviour.

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old anorexia nervosa inpatient hates the ward environment and decides to comply with feeding protocols to reach target weight and get out.
questions.explanation: This is escape conditioning (negative reinforcement), a form of aversive conditioning, where compliance removes the aversive ward environment.

questions.question_text: A 10-year-old boy is taught not to respond to TV noise while doing homework as the stimulus is not significant.
questions.explanation: Habituation is decreased response to a repeated, non-significant stimulus.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man, after being criticized for laziness, realizes his fault and next day seeks employment at a career centre.
questions.explanation: Insight learning is the sudden understanding and problem solution after reflection.

questions.question_text: Catatonia was first described by:
questions.explanation:
In 1882, Karl Kahlbaum, who was a German psychiatrist, coined the
terminology cyclothymia.

questions.question_text: Cycloid psychosis was introduced by:
questions.explanation:
In this condition, the psychotic symptoms appear suddenly a few days
before menstruation, resolve with the onset of menstrual bleeding and reappear with

questions.question_text: Dementia praecox was coined by:
questions.explanation:
In 1896, Emil Kraepelin grouped together catatonia, hebephrenia and
the deteriorating paranoid psychosis under the name of dementia praecox

questions.question_text: Hebephrenia was first described by:
questions.explanation: In 1871, this was described by Hecker.

questions.question_text: The term schizophrenia was introduced by:
questions.explanation:
In 1911, Bleuler introduced the term schizophrenia, applied it to
Kraepelin’s cases of dementia praecox and expanded the concept to include what
today may be considered to be schizophrenia spectrum disorders

questions.question_text: Schizoaffective disorder was introduced by:

questions.question_text: After 18 months of treatment, the patient stops medication. His mother wants to know the risk of relapse in percentage.
questions.explanation: If medication is stopped after 18 months, the relapse risk is about 75% within 1–2 years.
